opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think that's one of the most valuable things about games, especially when you start young. I played chess very seriously as a kid, and what chess teaches you, really brutally, is that when you lose, it's almost always your fault. There's no luck involved. You can't blame the dice or the referee. You have to sit there afterwards and go through the game and figure out where your thinking went wrong. That's quite a painful process, but it's incredibly formative, because it trains you to look at your own mistakes honestly and analytically rather than emotionally.

So I'd say losing should be treated as information. The emotion is natural, and actually I think you should care deeply about winning. If you don't care, you won't push yourself. But once the game is over, you have to switch modes and become almost a scientist about your own performance: what was my plan, where did I misjudge the position, was it a calculation error or a deeper conceptual misunderstanding? The players who improve fastest are the ones who can do that post-mortem without their ego getting in the way.

And winning has its own lessons, which people sometimes overlook. It's very easy to win and assume everything you did was right, when actually your opponent just made a bigger mistake. So I've always tried to analyse wins just as critically as losses. That's carried over into how I think about research at DeepMind. When an experiment works, you still have to ask why it worked, and whether you really understand it, or whether you got lucky.

The other thing games teach you is resilience. In a chess tournament you might lose a crushing game in the morning and have to sit down and play again in the afternoon. You have to learn to put that loss away, reset, and bring your full focus to the next game. That ability to compartmentalise disappointment and keep going is, I think, one of the most important skills you can have in any ambitious endeavour, whether it's science or building a company. You're going to fail far more often than you succeed, so you'd better have a healthy relationship with losing.

r001.rationale: The response treats losses as information and recommends analyzing mistakes to improve, but does not clearly say to channel the negative feelings of losing into motivation for specific improvements.

r002.rationale: The response discusses learning and resilience, but does not identify personal improvement, rather than winning or losing, as the source of meaning in competition.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the thing that games teach you — and I started with chess very young, I was playing competitively from about four or five — is that you get this very fast, very honest feedback loop. You make a decision, and the consequences of that decision play out in front of you, and there's nobody else to blame. In chess especially, there's no luck. If you lose, it's because you made a mistake somewhere, or your opponent understood something you didn't. And I think learning to sit with that, to actually look back at the game afterwards and find the moment where it went wrong, rather than making excuses — that's an incredibly useful habit for life, and certainly for science.

The other thing is that you learn to lose a lot. If you're playing seriously, you lose constantly, to people better than you, and you have to come back the next day and play again. So you develop a kind of resilience, but I'd say it's a specific kind — it's not just toughness, it's the ability to separate the result from your sense of yourself. The result is data. It's information about where your understanding is incomplete. And winning, interestingly, can be more dangerous than losing, because when you win you often don't examine the game as carefully, and you can carry forward bad habits that happened to work that time.

I think martial arts is similar in a lot of ways, maybe even more visceral, because the feedback is physical. But in both cases the real lesson is the same — it's about the process rather than the outcome. You train your decision-making under pressure, with time running out, with incomplete information about what the other person is thinking. And then ideally, over years, that becomes a kind of calm. You can be in a very intense situation and still think clearly. That's what I try to carry into running DeepMind, honestly — when things are going badly on a project, or there's a setback, the chess training kicks in and you think, okay, what's the position actually, what are the candidate moves, let's not panic.

astra-6.text:
I think the most valuable thing is learning to separate the result from the quality of what you did. In chess, you can win a game having played quite badly, or lose a game in which you played well and your opponent simply played better. If you only look at the outcome, you miss the lesson.

Losing is particularly useful because it forces you to confront gaps in your understanding. But you have to be willing to look at the game honestly, without making excuses or turning a mistake into a judgment about yourself. You made a bad decision; that doesn’t mean you’re incapable of making a better one next time.

I think martial arts can teach a similar humility, alongside emotional control and respect for your opponent. Winning should give you confidence, but also an appreciation of how much there still is to learn. Ideally, competition teaches you to care deeply and put everything into the effort, while still being able to step back afterward and ask, ‘What can I learn from that?’

r001.rationale: The response says losing can reveal gaps and mistakes to learn from, but it does not describe channeling negative feelings into motivation for specific improvements.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes learning and improving through competition, and says the outcome matters less than the quality of the effort and what can be learned.

sol-6.1.text:
I think both are valuable because they give you very honest feedback. You can have an idea of how good you are, but when you sit across the chessboard from someone, that idea gets tested. And learning to accept that—to say, “I made a mistake; what can I learn from it?”—is a very useful habit beyond chess.

Losing can teach you a great deal, provided you’re willing to look at it honestly. You want to separate the disappointment from the analysis. It should hurt a little if you care, but it shouldn’t become a judgment about your worth as a person.

Winning requires reflection too. You can win while making mistakes, and if you only study your losses, you can miss weaknesses that a stronger opponent would expose. Ideally, you develop the confidence to compete wholeheartedly and the humility to keep learning, whatever the result.
